Welcome! These pages are the practical, hands-on side of **MECH 501/600 —
Computational Turbulence**. Where the lectures build the theory, here you will
*use* it: refresh your scientific Python, get onto the course computing cluster,
and work through tutorials that combine turbulence theory, OpenFOAM simulations,
and Python post-processing.

## How it all fits together

The **lectures** develop the equations and models. These **tutorials** put them
to work: you will run simulations, post-process the results in **Python**, and
often do so on the **cluster**. Each tutorial contains numbered **Tasks** —
derivations, plots, and short discussions — which you collect into a single PDF
and upload to **Crowdmark** by the posted deadline.

If your Python or command-line skills feel rusty, work through the
[Python](python/index.qmd) section and get comfortable with the
[Cluster](cluster/index.qmd) before the first tutorial that needs them — it will
make everything afterwards much smoother.

**OpenFOAM** is the open-source CFD toolbox we use for the simulation side of the
course. It solves the RANS equations you meet in the lectures on real geometries.
The [OpenFOAM how-to](openfoam/how-to.qmd) walks you through your first case from
setup to post-processing — no prior CFD-software experience assumed.

## Working through a tutorial

1. Read the background and **run the provided code yourself** — don't just read it.
2. Answer every **Task** box (derivations, plots, short written answers).
3. Export your answers as a **single PDF** and upload it to Crowdmark before the deadline.

## What you'll need

- **Python** ≥ 3.10 with `numpy`, `matplotlib`, `scipy` (and later `pyvista` / `fluidfoam`).
- **OpenFOAM** — see the [OpenFOAM how-to](openfoam/how-to.qmd).
- An account on the **course cluster** — see the [Cluster](cluster/index.qmd) page.

Everything above is already installed in the cluster's JupyterLab environment, so
if you work there you can skip local setup entirely.

::: {.callout-tip}
